record.original_question: Suppose f and g are non-constant meromorphic functions that share four distinct values, and one of those four shared values is shared by counting multiplicities, meaning that for that one value the two functions take the value at exactly the same points with the same multiplicities, while for the other three values only the sets of shared points are assumed to coincide. Must the conclusion of Nevanlinna's Four-Value Theorem still follow, namely that after relabelling the values the cross-ratio (a1, a2, a3, a4) equals -1, a1 and a2 are Picard values of both functions, and g is a Mobius transformation of f that fixes a3 and a4 and permutes a1 and a2?

evidence.quote: Four-Value-Theorem (Nevanlinna [13]). Let f and g be non-constant meromorphic functions sharing values aν (1 ≤ ν ≤ 4), but now specifically by counting multiplicities. Then (relabelling the values, if necessary) (a1, a2, a3, a4) = (f, g, a3, a4) = -1 holds. In particular, a1 and a2 are Picard values of f and g, and g is a Mobius transformation of f that fixes a3 and a4 and permutes a1 and a2.
All attempts to prove or disprove a (1+3)-Theorem failed up to now (January 2011).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let f and g be non-constant meromorphic functions on the complex plane. For a value a ∈ ℂ ∪ {∞}, say that f and g share a IM (ignoring multiplicities) if f^{-1}(a) = g^{-1}(a) as sets, and share a CM (counting multiplicities) if in addition every point z₀ in this common preimage is a zero of f − a (interpreted appropriately at ∞) of the same multiplicity as it is for g − a.

Nevanlinna's Four-Value Theorem states: if f and g are non-constant meromorphic functions sharing four distinct values a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄ ∈ ℂ ∪ {∞} all CM, then (after relabelling) the cross-ratio (a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄) = −1, the values a₁ and a₂ are Picard exceptional values of both f and g, and g is a Möbius transformation of f that fixes a₃ and a₄ and interchanges a₁ and a₂.

Question (the (1+3) Four-Value Problem): Suppose f and g are non-constant meromorphic functions that share four distinct values a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄, where one of these values is shared CM and the remaining three are shared IM. Must the same conclusion as in Nevanlinna's Four-Value Theorem hold — namely, that after relabelling, (a₁, a₂, a₃, a₄) = −1, a₁ and a₂ are Picard values of both f and g, and g is a Möbius transformation of f fixing a₃, a₄ and permuting a₁, a₂?
artifact.status_search_result: The general (1+3) four-value problem (also known as Gundersen's question, equivalent to whether 3 IM + 1 CM forces 4 CM) remains open. Partial results exist; in particular, a 2024 work establishes the conclusion under the additional hypothesis that at least one of f, g has finite order. The unrestricted case is still unresolved.

status_evidence.title: On a question of Gary G. Gundersen concerning meromorphic functions sharing three distinct values IM and a fourth value CM
status_evidence.snippet: Suppose that f and g are two distinct and non-constant meromorphic functions, and one of f and g has finite order. If f and g share a1,a2,a3 IM and a4 CM, then f and g share a1,a2,a3,a4 CM.
status_evidence.claim: A finite-order partial resolution exists, but the general (1+3) four-value problem is still acknowledged to be unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Uniqueness of meromorphic functions sharing four values IM and one CM
status_evidence.snippet: Uniqueness of meromorphic functions sharing four values IM and one CM.
status_evidence.claim: Ongoing literature confirms the problem area as actively studied with partial results.
